source.author: stat
source.text: dumque uter angustae squalentia iugera Dirces verteret aut Tyrii solio non altus ovaret exsulis ambigitur, periit ius fasque bonumque et vitae mortisque pudor, quo tenditis iras, a, miseri r quid si peteretur crimine tanto limes uterque poli, quem Sol emissus Eoo cardine, quem portu vergens prospectat Hibero, quasque procul terras obliquo sidere tangit avius aut borea gelidas madidive tepentes igne noti?
source.text_original: dumque uter angustae squalentia iugera Dirces / verteret aut Tyrii solio non altus ovaret / exsulis ambigitur, periit ius fasque bonumque / et vitae mortisque pudor, quo tenditis iras, / a, miseri r quid si peteretur crimine tanto / limes uterque poli, quem Sol emissus Eoo / cardine, quem portu vergens prospectat Hibero, / quasque procul terras obliquo sidere tangit / avius aut borea gelidas madidive tepentes / igne noti?
source.text_english: And while it was debated which of the two should turn the foul acres of narrow Dirce, or, not far below the throne of Tyrius the exile, rejoice, right and justice and goodness perished, and the decency of life and death. To what point do you drive your anger, ah, wretched men? What if by so great a crime both boundaries of the sky were sought, the one which the sun, risen from the eastern gate, gazes on, the one which, leaning toward the Iberian harbor, he gazes on, and the lands far away which the wandering star touches with slanting course, whether by the cold north wind or by the southern blast, wet or warm with fire?
